acid: Strong mineral acid able to disolve almost anything, including most metals.
alembics: Alembics are alchemical stills that are used to refine or transmute liquids by distillation. An alembic is an alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distillation of liquids.
arms: Metal weapons and armours used by the constables patrolling in the town or guarding valuables. Arms are used to increase the efficacy and efficiency of these activities.
axes: The steel axe represents an advancement from plain metal tools. Useful for chopping trees and wood. Axe generally consists of an axe head with a handle.
beer: Beer comes in firkin casks of 8 gallons and is desired by all tiers of society. Brewed from malted grains. Beer is an alcoholic beverage produced by the brewing and fermentation of starches from cereal grains.
bellows: Bellows are crucial for maintaining the intense heat required in forges and furnaces. These tools are indispensable for blacksmiths, as they allow the controlled flow of air to stoke the fires to the temperatures needed for metalworking and smelting, especially when it comes to the process of steel-making.
bells: Bells are large vessels cast in metal, usually a bronze alloy of copper and tin, typically fashioned in specialized casting pits using complex clay molds. They function as the community's primary signaling system or for announcing religious services. These resonant instruments were often inscribed with prayers and mounted in high timber frames to project their sound across the surrounding parish.
belts: A belt is a flexible band or strap, typically made of leather or heavy cloth, worn around the natural waist or near it (as far down as the hips). Belts are used variously to secure or hold up clothing.
blades: Sharp blades made from iron and steel, often with a softer iron core for flexibility and a steel edge for increased sharpness and durability. Blades can be used directly as shears or as a component of various tools.
books: Religious books are significant cultural and artistic objects. In addition to the texts they hold, they are also considered sacred objects that functioned as tools for liturgy, private devotion, and the preservation of divine knowledge.
bread: Staple food desired by all tiers of the population. Baked from milled grains. Bread can be served at many temperatures. It is most commonly eaten with the hands, either by itself or as a carrier for other foods.
bricks: Important construction material required by many buildings. Burned from local clay at the brickworks. Fired bricks are one of the longest-lasting and strongest building materials.
bronze ingots: Ingots made of bronze alloy of copper and tin, cast in a regular shape to facilitate storage and transport.
butter: Desirable food by all tiers of the population which makes other food products tastier and more nutritious. Butter is a dairy product made from the fat and protein components of churned cream. It generally has a pale yellow colour but varies from deep yellow to nearly white. Its natural, unmodified colour is dependent on the source animal's feed.
candles: A candle is an ignitable wick embedded in wax, or another flammable solid substance such as tallow, that provides light, and in some cases, a fragrance. A candle can also provide heat or a method of keeping time.
canvas: A coarse, heavy-duty fabric woven from strong flax or hemp fibres in a dense tabby weave. Its exceptional strength and resistance to tearing make it the ideal material for the sails of cogs and hulks, as well as for the sturdy sacks and covers required for long-distance trade.
casks: A barrel or cask is a hollow cylindrical container with a bulging centre, longer than it is wide. Barrels have a variety of uses, including storage of liquids such as water, oil, and alcohol.
cattle: Large animals living on pasture land. Important source of meat. As draft animals, they pull carts and farm implements.
charcoal: Wood processed into nearly pure carbon. Burns better and at higher temperature due to reduced moisture content, making an important fuel for smelting and forging of metals.
chisels: A chisel is a wedged hand tool with a characteristically shaped cutting edge on the end of its blade, for carving or cutting a hard material (e.g. wood, stone, or metal).
cheese: Cheese is a welcome addition to the diet of the whole population. Made from fermented sheep or cow milk.
clay: Clay is a type of fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals. Clays develop plasticity when wet but can be hardened through firing. Clay is the ceramic material for making pottery and also useful material for building.
cloth: Textile fibres weaved into cloth are useful for a wide range of things, from clothing to making sails for windmills or ships.
coats: A coat is typically an outer garment for the upper body, worn by any gender for warmth. Coats typically have long sleeves and are open down the front, and closed by buttons, a belt, or a combination of some of these.
cog: Clinker built trade-ships, built to efficiently transport all kinds of cargo.
copper ingots: Refined copper ready to be worked into various useful items.
cookware: Sturdy vessels used for cooking, demanded by all tiers of the population.
copper ore: Ore containing copper dug from the copper mines and crushed for transportation.
cured fish: A vital export of the coastal reaches, fish preserved through salting or air-drying provides a lasting harvest from the unpredictable sea. The curing process ensures that this lean protein can endure the drafty holds of trade-ships and the long haul to inland parishes. Desired by all tiers of society cured fish is a testament to the mastery of salt and wind over the perishability of the catch.
cured meat: Produced by application of salt or suspension in the smokehouse, cured meat is the essential provision for long journeys and winter stores. The process draws out moisture, halting the natural decay of the flesh and infusing it with a savory character. Packed into sturdy casks, these sides of salted pork or smoked venison are highly valued by constables on patrol and merchants traversing the great distances between towns, offering a reliable source of protein when fresh meat is out of reach.
donations: Purchased from the church to achieve salvation (ie. more prestige).
dye: A dye is a coloured substance. The majority dyes are derived from non-animal sources such as roots, berries, bark, leaves, wood, fungi and lichens.
dyed cloth: A textile which is treated with dye using sources such as roots, berries, bark, leaves, wood, fungi and lichens.
dyed yarn: Woolen yarn which is treated with dye using sources such as roots, berries, bark, leaves, wood, fungi and lichens.
fish: Fish is a sought after food and important source of proteins and vitamins in what for most is overwhelmingly a grain based diet. Untreated fish perishes quickly, so it is often salted for storage or transportation.
firewood: Firewood is a primary source of energy, used to power a wide range of operations that require heating as well as by all the inhabitants of the town. It is readily and cheaply available near forest, but its voluminous nature makes it expensive to transport.
flax fibres: Flax is a flowering plant and used for producing textiles (like for bed sheets, underclothes, table linen etc). Flax oil is known as linseed oil.
flax plants: Flax is a flowering plant that is cultivated for both its seeds and fibers and, occasionally, cut flowers. With a long history of cultivation, the fibres of the flax plant are used to make linen cloth for clothing, and for making ropes. The seeds can also be extracted and used as foor for animals or humans.
fleece: The raw, unwashed bounty of the pasture, fleece is the thick coat of wool sheared from the parish's sheep. Heavy with natural lanolin and redolent of the damp earth and clover of the fields, these curly locks are the starting point for all fine textiles. Before it can be spun, the fleece must undergo the backbreaking labour of cleaning and carding to align its fibers. Whether destined for the humble tunics of the commoners or the richly dyed robes of the nobility, fleece is the versatile material that keeps the population warm against the elements.
flour: Flour is made by milling seeds of grain, preserving the nutrional value while making it easier to use for baking.
glass ingots: Glass is an amorphous solid. Due to its ease of formability into any shape, glass can be used for vessels, such as bowls, vases, bottles, jars and drinking glasses.
furniture: Objects intended to support various human activities such as seating (stools, chairs, and sofas etc), eating (tables), storing items, working, and sleeping (beds).
garments: Items worn on the body. Garments can insulate against cold or hot conditions, and it can provide a hygienic barrier, keeping infectious and toxic materials away from the body.
gears: Wooden gears made out of a central hub connected by thick spokes to a segmented rim, into which carved wooden pegs or cogs are mortised. The cogs are intentionally designed to be replaceable when worn down by the relentless grinding of transferring power. Lubrication with a grease coating can make the power transmission more efficient and reduce the wear.
glassware: Drinkware and tableware used to set a table for eating a meal and generally glass items such as vases, and glasses used for many different purposes.
gold bars: Refined gold ready to be worked into valuable items or minted into coins. Gold bars are highly valuable and should be well protected.
gold ore: Ore containing gold dug from the gold mines and crushed for transportation.
grain: The lifeblood of the parish, these dried seeds of cereal grasses are harvested from the sun-drenched fields of the grain farm. Whether destined for the miller's stones to become the commoners' daily bread or the malthouse to be steeped for the town's brewing, grain remains the foundational staple that sustains every household, from the humblest tenant to the local gentry.
grindstones: Grindstones are used to sharpen tools made of metal. Grindstones are usually made from sandstone.
ham: Ham is produced by curing raw pork by salting, brining, also known as wet curing, or smoking.
handcart: Manually operated cart for trade with neighbouring towns. Handcarts are simple and small vehicles, but they are useful for land transportation. Their low cost of production and maintenance makes them reliable for entrepreneurs with small funds. The making of handcarts is light on materials, given their simplistic nature. A few pieces of timber are enough to create this vehicle, as it's a small one, but that doesn't mean it isn't a complicated one. Due to its intricate details it requires a moderate amount of work to produce, but its usefulness is unrivaled.
harnesses: Harnesses made from wood and leather are made to fit comfortably on work-animals, allowing them to more easily pull their load.
health: The health of the population can influence population growth. Each health point generated in a town corresponds to one fully healthy household. The overall coverage percentage when combining all sources of health gives the health level of the town.
herbs: Herbs have a variety of uses including culinary, medicinal, aromatic and in some cases, spiritual.
hides: An animal skin treated for human use. Animal skins are usually processed fresh or salted and tanned.
hinges: Sturdy pivots are essential for the operation of any gated or shuttered structure. From the heavy timber doors of a noble's mansion to the delicate windows of a merchant's townhouse, hinges allow for the controlled passage of light, air, and inhabitants. Their creak is a sensory marker of a well-ordered household, and when applied to the heavy bellows of a forge, they enable the steady, focused intake of air required to stoke the hottest fires.
honey: Honey is a sweet and viscous substance made by several species of bees. Bees are stockpiled honey in the hive.
hop beer: Hop beer is an alcoholic beverage produced by the brewing and fermentation of starches from cereal grains.
hulk: Large two-masted, clinker built trade-ships, built to efficiently transport all kinds of cargo over long distances.
iron ore: Rocks and minerals from which metallic iron can be extracted. The ores are usually rich in iron oxides and vary in coulor from dark grey, bright yellow, or deep purple to rusty red.
jewellery: Jewellery consists of decorative items worn for personal adornment. Jewellery may be made from a wide range of materials.
labour: Manual labour, predominantly offered by the commoners of the town. Almost all production recipes require this, with the basic recipes being the most labour intensive and more sophisticated ones requiring less labour input.
lathes: The lathe is the master craftsman's engine for creating precision-turned components from wood and metal. By rotating the workpiece at a steady speed, it allows the artisan to use sharp steel chisels to carve perfectly symmetrical forms, such as the felloes of a spinning wheel or the blocks of a tackle. This technical mastery over shape and balance is fundamental to the production of sophisticated tools and machinery, elevating the craft from mere manual labour to a science of rotation and refined measurement.
lead bars: Lead is soft and malleable, and also has a relatively low melting point.
lead ore: Lead is easily extracted from its ores. Galena is a principal ore of lead which often bears silver.
leather: Leather is a strong, flexible and durable material. Leather can be used to make a variety of items, including clothing, footwear, handbags, furniture, tools etc.
light armour: Used to protect an object, individual, especially direct contact weapons or projectiles during combat, or from a potentially dangerous environment or activity.
limestone: Type of carbonate sedimentary rock which is the main source of the material lime. Limestone often contains fossils.
lodging: Lodging describes accommodation for sleep, rest, food, safety, shelter from cold temperatures or rain, storage etc. Lodging is offered by an owner of property.
logs: Logs of lumber from cut trees. Lumber can be used as a crude construction material or, more frequently, sawed into timber boards or breams.
looms: The loom is a large device used for weaving large sheets of cloth. A treadle loom also features a foot pedal, called treadle, which is attached to a complex mechanical system consisting of levers and pulleys that allows some of the warp threads to be raised when the treadle is pushed down. This allows the weaver to simply pass the shuttle through the already separated warp threads, accelerating the tedious weaving process.
malt: Any cereal grain that has been made to germinate by soaking in water and then stopped from germinating further by drying with hot air, a process known as malting.
manure: Organic matter that is used as organic fertiliser in agriculture. Manures contribute to the fertility of soil by adding organic matter and nutrients.
meat: Sought after addition to the diet. Tasty but spoils quickly and can't be transported for trade, unless preserved with salt.
medicine: Foul tasting liquid, believed to have healing powers. Sought after by the upper tiers of the population.
milk: Milk is an agricultural product, dairy milk is collected from farm animals. Milk is processed into a variety of products such as cream, butter etc.
mouldboards: A tool used for farming. Its function is loosening or turning the soil before sowing seed or planting.
nails: Nails are made by hammering iron into a thin and sharp shape, with a head for holding. They are used for fastening wood and other materials then can be hammered through together. Because of the labour involved in forging nails, and the utility they provide, nails are considered a particularly valuable commodity.
nets: A net comprises threads or yarns knotted and twisted into a grid-like structure which blocks the passage of large items, while letting small items and fluids pass.
ox power: Yoked oxen offer strength and power that far surpasses that of a human. This is useful for pulling ploughs or powering machinery or bellows.
paper: Paper is a medium for writing texts, either as books or as separate sheets.
pasties: Baked pastry which consists of barley flour and uncooked filling, typically meat and vegetables, baked in a folded and crimped circle.
pickaxes: Pickaxes are strong tools made from steel for extra hardness, allowing them to efficiently pick apart rocks and ores.
pies: A pie is a baked dish which is usually made of a pastry dough casing that contains a filling of various sweet or savoury ingredients.
plate armour: Armour made of steel plates designed to deflect the most blows. Though expensive to obtain it offers great protection in battle, and prestige, for those who can afford to brandish it.
ploughs: Ploughs are heavy chunks of wood cut into shape, with handles. If possible, an iron point is attached, called plough-share. It is heavy enough to require a strong animal, like an ox, to be pulled. An improved design adds a mould-board behind the plough-share, which turns the furrow over as it slices into the ground. It gives the opportunity to utilise heavier soil, as well as providing better drainage.
potash: A white caustic salt obtained by leaching the ashes of burned hardwood in large vats.
protection: Protection is any measure taken to guard a thing against damage caused by outside forces.
raw cloth: Freshly cut from the loom, raw cloth is the coarse, unrefined result of the weaver's rhythmic shuttle. While it possesses the interlocked strength of the yarn—be it wool or flax—it remains stiff and contains the natural oils and impurities of the fiber. Before it can be tailored into garments or coats, it must be sent to the fulling house to be beaten and cleaned in the presence of fuller's earth, a process that shrinks and thickens the fabric into a soft, durable material suitable for the town's tailors and the gentry's wardrobes.
resin: Wood resin is gathered from live trees and can be mixed with charcoal dust to make wood tar.
rigging: Encompassing both the standing rigging, the mast and stays holding it in position, as well as the running rigging used to power and control the ships, the sails, the halyards to hoist them, the sheets to hold their shape.
rope: A rope is a group of yarns, plies, fibres, or strands that are twisted or braided together into a larger and stronger form. Ropes have tensile strength and so can be used for dragging and lifting.
sails: Sail is a tensile structure, which is made from fabric or other materials, that uses wind power to propel sailing craft.
salt: Salt is a mineral composed primarily of sodium chloride. Salt is essential for life in general, and saltiness is one of the basic human tastes.
sculptures: Sculpture is the three-dimensional art work which is physically presented in the dimensions of height, width and depth.
scythes: A scythe is an agricultural hand tool for mowing grass or harvesting crops. It is used to cut down or reap edible grains, before the process of threshing.
seeds: Plant seeds are both rich in oil and nutritious, though hard to digest for humans. Used as fodder for animals or can be ground down for the oil content.
silver bars: Silver bars have been produced to mint coins, make valuable accessories etc and have been used as a means of payment in trade and as a store of value.
silver ore: Rocks and minerals containing silver, often found alongside lead in vertical fissures of the earth.
slaked lime: A soft, white, crystalline, very slightly water-soluble powder, obtained by the action of water on lime: used mainly in mortars, plasters, and cements.
snekkja: Sleek ships originally designed by vikings, with the name meaning snake. Good for short to medium distance trade and fishing.
soap: A cleansing agent produced by the chemical reaction of fats with caustic lye. Highly valued for its ability to remove grease and impurities, it is essential for the laundering of textiles and the maintenance of a well-ordered household.
spirits: Liquid of nearly pure alcohol, most suitable as a solvent for various solutes.
spinning wheels: The spinning wheel replaces the slow labour of the drop spindle with a treadle-driven pull. Crafted by the carpenter with the aid of a lathe, its large wheel and delicate flyer allow for the continuous twisting of fleece or flax into fine, uniform thread. The steady hum of the spindle is the sensory backdrop to the production of the yarn that feeds the town's looms, significantly increasing the output of the textile parish.
steel ingots: Piece of steel that has been formed into a particular shape to make it easier for transportation and storage. Steel ingots are made by melting the metal and then reforming the shape in a mould.
stockfish: Stockfish is unsalted fish dried by cold air and wind on wooden racks on the foreshore. The method is cheap and effective in suitable climates; the work can be done by the fisherman and family, and the resulting product is easily transported to market.
swords: A sword is an edged, bladed weapon intended for manual cutting or thrusting. Its blade, longer than a knife, is attached to a hilt and can be straight or curved.
tackles: A sophisticated arrangement of pulleys and ropes, tackles allow for the lifting of immense weights that would otherwise defy human effort. Assembled at the pulleyworks using seasoned wooden blocks and high-tensile rope, these devices are indispensable in the grueling work of the iron mines and stone quarries. By distributing the load across multiple lines, the pull of a few commoners can hoist massive blocks of limestone or heavy buckets of ore from the deep, damp pits of the earth.
tallow: Rendered animal fat, typically harvested from the butchery and purified through boiling. This versatile substance is the primary fuel for the commoners' candles and serves as an essential lubricant for the wooden gears and tackles of the town's machinery.
tapestries: Heavy, decorative textiles woven or embroidered with intricate scenes of history or devotion. Beyond their artistic merit and the prestige they bring to a household, these thick hangings serve a practical purpose by insulating the cold stone walls of mansions and cathedrals against the winter chill.
tar: Wood tar is made from crushed charcoal mixed with wood resin. It makes an excellent substance for water-proofing wood constructions or ships. It's also extremely foul tasting, meaning it's sure to have healing properties that can be used medicinally.
thread: A thread is a long strand of material, often composed of several filaments or fibres, used for joining, creating or decorating textiles.
tiles: Tiles are usually thin, square or rectangular coverings manufactured from hard-wearing material. Tiles are often used to form wall and floor coverings, and can range from simple square tiles to complex or mosaics.
timber: Processed timber boards and beams, ready for use in construction or production.
tin ingots: Refined tin cast into a manageable form for transport and trade. This soft, silvery-white metal is highly resistant to corrosion and is most valued for its role in creating bronze, though it can also be used to line cookware to prevent the leaching of base metals.
tin ore: Partially crushed heavy and dark-coloured tin ore.
tools: Metal tools for increasing the efficiency and output in a wide variety of production recipes.
tumbrel: The tumbrels are moderately sized vehicles, which makes them very relevant methods of land transportation. They're fairly easy to produce and maintain, making them very good vehicle options. They can carry all types of goods, and they can carry a good amount of merchandise, meaning they're very useful for trading. These carriages require powerful oxen to move them, but that's what gives them their immense power. They're quite complex machines, which means their production requires multiple components and a good amount of work. Timber is required to make the base of the carriage as its high strength helps in carrying a big amount of goods. Then, wheels are carefully attached to the main part to enable the movement. This process requires precision and quality tools, otherwise the wheels might get stuck.
varnish: A clear, protective liquid prepared by dissolving resin into a solvent. When applied to fabrics or wood it oxides and forms a wind and water-resistant layer that preserves the underlying material from degradation and rot.
wax: Natural wax produced by honey bees. Wax is used as a lubricant and waterproofing agent, as a polish for wood and leather, for making candles.
wheels: A wheel is a rotating component (typically circular in shape) that is intended to turn on an axle bearing.
wine: Wine is an alcoholic drink made from fermented fruit. Different varieties of grapes and strains of yeasts are major factors in different styles of wine.
windows: A window is an opening in a wall, door or roof that allows the exchange of light and may also allow the passage of sound and sometimes air.
wool: Wool is sheared from sheep, then cleaned and carded, aligning the fibers to prepare them for spinning. After being spun into yarn using a spindle or spinning wheel, the wool can be woven into fabrics or knitted into warm garments like cloaks, tunics, and stockings. Wool’s natural insulation makes it ideal for cold climates, providing warmth and comfort. In addition to clothing, wool is often used as upholstery for furniture, padding for mattresses, or even as tapestries that line castle walls. Its water-resistant qualities also make it useful for outerwear, such as capes and mantles, protecting travelers from the elements. Dyed with natural pigments, wool garments range from the everyday tunics of peasants to the richly colored robes of nobility.
wrought iron: Wrought iron is an iron alloy with a very low carbon content. It is highly refined, with a small amount of silicate slag forged out into fibres.
yarn: Yarn is a long continuous length of interlocked fibres, used in sewing, crocheting, knitting, weaving, embroidery, ropemaking, and the production of textiles
premium cheese: Premium cheese is made from sheep or cow milk fermented in a strictly controlled environment, with the exact details kept closely guarded by those that make it.
premium cog: The pinnacle of clinker-built naval architecture, the premium cog is a testament to the master shipwright's art. Utilizing the finest rot-resistant oak and reinforced with meticulous ironwork, this vessel is designed for the discerning merchant-adventurer who demands both speed and safety. Its broad beam and deep draft allow for a substantial cargo of wool or wine, while the refined rigging and superior sailcloth ensure it can catch the slightest breeze. To command such a vessel is a mark of significant prestige and household standing among the seafaring elite.
premium garments: Premium garments are produced from high quality materials and with great skill. Precious materials are often woven into the garments to give an unique and exclusive appearance.
premium glassware: Premium drinkware and tableware made from high quality glass, with fewer impurities and imperfections than regular glassware. Often adorned with precious materials to give an even more exclusive appearance and ensure guests remember your household as a prestigous one.
premium steel: Premium steel characterized by high carbon content and a pattern of bands that give it a characteristic look. The steel that has been formed into a particular shape to make it easier for transportation and storage. Steel ingots are made by melting the metal and then reforming the shape in a mould.
premium swords: Premium swords are made of higher quality materials and adorned with precious materials to give it an exclusive look.
premium sails: Premium sails are made from fabric or other materials of high quality and with great skill. They allow sailing crafts that use them to move swifter and with less effort than regular sails.
